FINDING_ID: LB_F001  
SEVERITY: 0.88  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.73  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer`/`Allocation` never validate that `task_id` and `model_id` are unique, but the public API treats them as unique keys. That silently corrupts results: with duplicate task IDs, `Allocation.model_load()` builds a dict keyed by `task_id` and can count the later task twice (`dup` with demands `1000` and `5000` produced load `10000`); with duplicate model IDs, `get_assigned_tasks()` uses `list.index()` and can report no assignments even when the second duplicate column is set.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Validate uniqueness of all `task_id` and `model_id` values at `LoadBalancer`/`Allocation` construction and raise `ValueError` on duplicates; then use the existing index maps for lookups instead of `list.index()`.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_F002  
SEVERITY: 0.82  
FLAW_CLASS: 1  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.68  
DESCRIPTION: `RoleAssignment.reassign()` is nondeterministic when the previous COL is inactive and two remaining candidates tie on adjusted COL score. It iterates `active_models` as a `set`, inserts scores into `col_scores` in that arbitrary order, then uses `max(col_scores, key=...)` with no tie-break. I verified this with the same logical inputs under different `PYTHONHASHSEED` values: one run chose `aa` as COL, another chose `bb`. That breaks reproducibility and can change downstream routing for identical evidence.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Replace the plain `max()` with a deterministic selection that includes the converged tie-break rule, e.g. choose by `(adjusted_score, _tie_break_key(model))`, and sort `active_models` before scoring.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_F003  
SEVERITY: 0.79  
FLAW_CLASS: 5  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.58  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer` accepts negative `Task.token_demand`, which lets one task create fake capacity for another. Verified with a single model at `L=1000`: assigning tasks `-500` and `1200` yielded a final reported load of `700`, so the oversized task was accepted only because the negative-demand task reduced `current_loads` first. That makes the core capacity constraint manipulable by malformed input.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Validate `Task` and `ModelSpec` numerics at construction or in `LoadBalancer.__init__`: require finite non-negative `token_demand`, finite non-negative `L_std`, positive finite `L`/`tau`, and `criticality` in `[0, 1]`.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_F004  
SEVERITY: 0.74  
FLAW_CLASS: 5  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.66  
DESCRIPTION: `RoleAssignment.reassign()` decides whether a COL should exist from `len(self._models)` instead of the current active pool size. If a 3-model run degrades to two active models, reassignment still emits `PM + COL` even though initial assignment explicitly treats `K < 3` as “no COL.” I verified this by starting with three homogeneous models, shrinking the active set to `{PM, one other}`, and observing `{'m0': PM, 'm1': COL}`. That breaks the intended K=2 reduction after failures.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Base the COL-exists decision on `len(active_models)`, not the original pool size; when fewer than 3 models are active, assign all non-PM models as `PAR`.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_F005  
SEVERITY: 0.68  
FLAW_CLASS: 5  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.49  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer.validate_homogeneous()` does not actually validate the stated homogeneous reduction. It only returns the loose `balanced` predicate, and with default `epsilon_bal=0.1` that can pass obviously skewed allocations. Verified with `k=2`: PM exclusion sent both equal tasks to the lone PAR model (`[[0,1],[0,1]]`, loads `[0, 2000]`), yet `balanced` still returned `True`. This means the reduction test can certify a broken homogeneous case and masks the still-live PM-exclusion distortion.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Make the validator check the actual expected homogeneous property: near-equal load across admissible executors, or exact distribution for the constructed symmetric case; do not reuse the broad runtime tolerance as a proof condition.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_F006  
SEVERITY: 0.63  
FLAW_CLASS: 5  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.46  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer.validate_k1()` also fails to validate its own claim. The docstring says K=1 reduction includes feasibility `sum b_j <= L1`, but the implementation only checks that every task was assigned to the single model. I verified that with `L=5000` and tasks `3000 + 4000`, the solver force-assigned both tasks, emitted an F1 overload warning, and the validator’s assignment-only condition still evaluated `True`.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Have `validate_k1()` assert both assignment coverage and no feasibility violations, e.g. by checking `alloc.model_load(...) <= L` or reusing `_check_feasibility()` and requiring zero F1/F3 violations.  
VERIFIED: TRUE
